title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 155 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 772–774 (Night 155, continuing directly from nights-154), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 155 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. The boatman sets ʿAlī and Abū al-Ḥasan ashore on the far bank of the Tigris, and the slave-girl turns back to the palace. ʿAlī can barely walk, and the place is unsafe at night, so Abū al-Ḥasan takes him to a trusted friend's house, explaining their late wandering with a story about a debtor who slipped away. In the morning they return to the city, and Abū al-Ḥasan brings ʿAlī to his own house, sends for musicians and friends and keeps a feast going into the night to lift his spirits. But when a singing-girl sings two lines on parted lovers, ʿAlī falls senseless until dawn; when he comes to, Abū al-Ḥasan sees him home, sits with him a while, and leaves him still in the grip of his passion. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu wa-al-khamsūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth-and-fifty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fifty-fifth night,
sentences.n: al-khāmisa, “the fifth”, is the ordinal, feminine to agree with layla; al-khamsūn, “fifty”, keeps its cardinal form and is joined by wa-.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْمَلَّاحَ قَذَفَ بِهِمَا إِلَى الْبَرِّ وَالْجَارِيَةُ مَعَهُمَا إِلَى أَنْ قَطَعُوا ذَلِكَ الْجَانِبَ وَعَدَوْا إِلَى الْبَرِّ الثَّانِي
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-mallāḥa qadhafa bihimā ilā al-barri wa-al-jāriyatu maʿahumā ilā an qaṭaʿū dhālika al-jāniba wa-ʿadaw ilā al-barri al-thānī
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the boatman rowed with-the-two toward the shore, and the slave-girl with-them-two, until they crossed-over that side and passed to the second shore.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the boatman rowed the two of them toward the shore, the slave-girl with them, until they had left that bank behind and crossed over to the other side.
sentences.n: qadhafa bihimā, “he rowed with them”, as at the end of the last night: bi- of accompaniment. wa-al-jāriyatu maʿahumā, “the slave-girl being with them”, is a circumstantial clause opened by wa-. ilā an, “until”, is followed here by a perfect, qaṭaʿū, because the crossing actually happened. qaṭaʿū and ʿadaw are masculine plural and take in the boatman, the two young men and the girl together. ʿadaw, “they crossed”, comes from ʿadā, “to pass beyond”; the fatḥa on its dāl is the print's own, and so is the shadda in الملّاح.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَا إِلَى الْبَرِّ وَطَلَعَا وَوَدَّعَتْهُمَا الْجَارِيَةُ وَقَالَتْ لَهُمَا كَانَ قَصْدِى لَا أُفَارِقُكُمَا لَكِنَّنِي لَا أَقْدِرُ أَنْ أَسِيرَ إِلَى مَكَانٍ غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ عَادَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-nazalā ilā al-barri wa-ṭalaʿā wa-waddaʿathumā al-jāriyatu wa-qālat lahumā kāna qaṣdī lā ufāriqukumā lākinnanī lā aqdiru an asīra ilā makānin ghayri hādhā al-mawḍiʿi thumma inna al-jāriyata ʿādat
sentences.l: And the-two went-down to the shore and went-up, and the slave-girl bade-them-two-farewell and said to-them-two: It-was my-intent (that) I-part-not-from-you-two, but I am-not able that I-go to a place other-than this spot. Then indeed the slave-girl went-back.
sentences.i: The two of them stepped out onto the shore and climbed the bank, and the slave-girl bade them farewell, saying, “I had meant not to leave you, but I cannot go anywhere beyond this spot.” Then she went back.
sentences.n: nazalā … wa-ṭalaʿā, “they got down … and went up”: down out of the boat, then up the bank. The print writes the final yāʾ of qaṣdī, “my intent”, as ى. kāna qaṣdī lā ufāriqukumā, “my intent was I do not leave you”: the clause follows with no an and with the indicative ufāriqu, looser than Classical an lā ufāriqakumā. ghayri, “other than”, is genitive in agreement with makānin, which it describes, and itself governs hādhā al-mawḍiʿi. thumma inna, “then indeed”, moves the tale on, and the girl drops out of the story.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ فَإِنَّهُ وَقَعَ مَطْرُوحًا بَيْنَ يَدَيْ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ لَا يَسْتَطِيعُ النُّهُوضَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin fa-innahu waqaʿa maṭrūḥan bayna yaday Abī al-Ḥasani lā yastaṭīʿu al-nuhūḍa
sentences.l: And as-for ʿAlī son of Bakkār, indeed he fell cast-down between the two-hands of Abū al-Ḥasan, not able (for) the rising.
sentences.i: As for ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, he fell down in a heap before Abū al-Ḥasan and could not get up.
sentences.n: wa-ammā … fa-, “and as for … then”: ammā sets up the topic, and fa- opens what is said about it. maṭrūḥan, “thrown down”, describes his state as he fell (accusative). bayna yaday, “between the two hands of”, means simply “in front of”; the dual yadāni drops its -ni before the following noun. The shadda in وامّا is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ إِنَّ هَذَا الْمَكَانَ غَيْرُ أَمِينٍ وَنَخْشَى عَلَى أَنْفُسِنَا مِنَ التَّلَفِ فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ بِسَبَبِ اللُّصُوصِ وَالْعَيَّارِينَ وَأَوْلَادِ الْحَرَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Abū al-Ḥasani inna hādhā al-makāna ghayru amīnin wa-nakhshā ʿalā anfusinā mina al-talafi fī hādhā al-makāni bi-sababi al-luṣūṣi wa-al-ʿayyārīna wa-awlādi al-ḥarāmi
sentences.l: So Abū al-Ḥasan said to-him: Indeed this place (is) not safe, and we-fear for our-selves from the ruin in this place by-reason-of the thieves and the ʿayyārs and the children of the forbidden.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said to him, “This place is not safe. We may well come to harm here, with the thieves and ruffians and scoundrels about.”
sentences.n: khashiya ʿalā … min, “to fear for … from”: ʿalā marks who is at risk, min the danger (al-talaf, “ruin, destruction”). The ʿayyārūn (here genitive, al-ʿayyārīn) were the street gangs of the medieval cities, toughs and sometimes outlaws. awlād al-ḥarām, “children of the forbidden”, i.e. bastards, is the common term of abuse for rogues. bi-sababi, “by reason of”: bi- of cause. The shadda in العيّارين is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَمَشَى قَلِيلًا وَهُوَ لَا يَسْتَطِيعُ الْمَشْىَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin wa-mashā qalīlan wa-huwa lā yastaṭīʿu al-mashya
sentences.l: So ʿAlī son of Bakkār rose and walked a-little, and he (was) not able (for) the walking.
sentences.i: So ʿAlī ibn Bakkār got up and walked a little way, though he was in no state to walk.
sentences.n: wa-huwa lā yastaṭīʿu, “and he not able”: a circumstantial clause, wa- with a pronoun, “while he could not”. The print writes al-mashy, “walking”, with final ى for ي.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ لَهُ فِي ذَلِكَ الْجَانِبِ أَصْدِقَاءُ فَقَصَدَ مَنْ يَثِقُ بِهِ مِنْهُمْ وَمَنْ يَأْنَسُ إِلَيْهِ فَدَقَّ بَابَهُ فَخَرَجَ إِلَيْهِ مُسْرِعًا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna Abū al-Ḥasani lahu fī dhālika al-jānibi aṣdiqāʾu fa-qaṣada man yathiqu bihi minhum wa-man yaʾnasu ilayhi fa-daqqa bābahu fa-kharaja ilayhi musriʿan
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan was — to-him on that side (were) friends; so he-made-for whom he-trusts in-him of-them and whom he-is-at-ease with-him, and he-knocked-on his-door, and he-came-out to-him hurrying.
sentences.i: Now Abū al-Ḥasan had friends on that side of the river, so he made for one of them whom he trusted and was at ease with, and knocked at his door; and the man came hurrying out to him.
sentences.n: kāna Abū al-Ḥasani lahu … aṣdiqāʾu, literally “Abū al-Ḥasan was — he had friends”: the subject is put first and the having follows as a clause of its own, a common pattern in the Nights. aṣdiqāʾu, “friends”, is diptote, so nominative -u without nunation. man … wa-man, “one whom … and whom”, is one friend described twice. wathiqa bi-, “to trust in”, and anisa ilā, “to be at ease with”: each verb chooses its preposition.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأٰهُمَا رَحَّبَ بِهِمَا وَدَخَلَ بِهِمَا إِلَى مَنْزِلِهِ وَأَجْلَسَهُمَا وَتَحَدَّثَ مَعَهُمَا وَسَأَلَهُمَا أَيْنَ كَانَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhumā raḥḥaba bihimā wa-dakhala bihimā ilā manzilihi wa-ajlasahumā wa-taḥaddatha maʿahumā wa-saʾalahumā ayna kānā
sentences.l: And when he-saw-the-two, he-welcomed the-two, and entered with-the-two into his-dwelling, and seated-them-two, and talked with-them-two, and asked-them-two where they-two-had-been.
sentences.i: When he saw them he made them welcome, took them into his house and gave them seats, talked with them, and asked them where they had been.
sentences.n: The print spells raʾāhumā, “he saw them”, with a single alif (رأهما) for the usual رآهما; the long ā is shown here with a small dagger alif. raḥḥaba bi-, “to welcome”, takes its object with bi-. dakhala bihimā, “he went in with them”, is “he took them in”: bi- of accompaniment makes the verb transitive. The shadda in تحدّث is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ قَدْ خَرَجْنَا فِي هَذَا الْوَقْتِ وَأَحْوَجَنَا إِلَى هَذَا الْأَمْرِ إِنْسَانٌ عَامَلْتُهُ وَلِي عِنْدَهُ دَرَاهِمُ وَبَلَغَنِي أَنَّهُ يُرِيدُ السَّفَرَ بِمَالِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Abū al-Ḥasani qad kharajnā fī hādhā al-waqti wa-aḥwajanā ilā hādhā al-amri insānun ʿāmaltuhu wa-lī ʿindahu darāhimu wa-balaghanī annahu yurīdu al-safara bi-mālī
sentences.l: So Abū al-Ḥasan said: We-have come-out at this time, and there-drove-us to this matter a person I-dealt-with-him, and to-me with-him (are) dirhams, and it-reached-me that he wants the journey with my-money.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan said, “We have come out at this hour because a man drove us to it: someone I have had dealings with, who holds money of mine, and I heard that he meant to leave town with it.
sentences.n: wa-aḥwajanā ilā hādhā al-amri insānun, “and a person drove us to this business”: the verb comes first, singular, then its object -nā and the phrase with ilā, and the subject insānun is held to the end, where it can take its description ʿāmaltuhu, “I had dealings with him”, a relative clause without alladhī, as is regular after an indefinite noun. aḥwaja, form IV, “to make (someone) need”. wa-lī ʿindahu darāhimu, “and I have dirhams with him”: he owes me money. bi-mālī, “with my money”: bi- of accompaniment. The whole story is a cover for where they have really been.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجْتُ فِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ وَقَصَدْتُهُ وَاسْتَأْنَسْتُ بِرَفِيقِى هَذَا عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَجِئْنَا لَعَلَّنَا نَنْظُرُهُ فَتَوَارَى مِنَّا وَلَمْ نَرَهُ وَعُدْنَا صِفْرَ الْيَدَيْنِ بِلَاشَيْءٍ
sentences.tr: fa-kharajtu fī hādhihi al-laylati wa-qaṣadtuhu wa-istaʾnastu bi-rafīqī hādhā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-jiʾnā laʿallanā nanẓuruhu fa-tawārā minnā wa-lam narahu wa-ʿudnā ṣifra al-yadayni bilā shayʾin
sentences.l: So I-went-out on this night and made-for-him, and I-took-comfort in my-companion this, ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and we-came, perhaps-we see-him; but he-hid from-us and we-did-not see-him, and we-returned empty of-the-two-hands, without-a-thing.
sentences.i: So I went out tonight to look for him, taking my friend here, ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, along for company, and we came in the hope of seeing him; but he kept out of our way and we never saw him, and we came back empty-handed, with nothing at all.
sentences.n: istaʾnasa bi-, “to take comfort in”: bi- marks the companion. The print writes rafīqī, “my companion”, with final ى. laʿallanā nanẓuruhu, “perhaps we might see him”: naẓara here takes its object directly and means “to see”, where Classical usage has naẓara ilā, “to look at”. tawārā min, “to hide from”. ṣifra al-yadayni, “empty of the hands”, describes their state (accusative). The print runs bilā shayʾ, “without a thing”, together (بلاشيء); it is kept and pointed as one word. The shadda in لعلّنا is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَشَقَّ عَلَيْنَا الْعَوْدُ فِي هَذَا الْوَقْتِ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ وَلَمْ نَدْرِ أَيْنَ نَسِيرُ فَجِئْنَا إِلَيْكَ لِمَا نَعْلَمُ مِنْ صَدَاقَتِكَ وَعَوَائِدِكَ الْجَمِيلَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-shaqqa ʿalaynā al-ʿawdu fī hādhā al-waqti mina al-layli wa-lam nadri ayna nasīru fa-jiʾnā ilayka li-mā naʿlamu min ṣadāqatika wa-ʿawāʾidika al-jamīlati
sentences.l: And hard-upon-us was the returning at this time of the night, and we-did-not know where we-go; so we-came to-you, for what we-know of your-friendship and your-customs the fine.
sentences.i: It was hard for us to go home at this hour of the night, and we did not know where to go, so we came to you, knowing your friendship and your kind ways.”
sentences.n: shaqqa ʿalā, “to be hard on someone”. lam nadri, “we did not know”: lam with the jussive of darā, which drops its final -ī. li-mā naʿlamu, “because of what we know”: li- of cause with mā, “what”, and min, “of”, spelling out what it is. ʿawāʾid is the plural of ʿāda, “custom, habit”; his “fine customs” are his known generosity.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُمَا مَرْحَبًا وَأَهْلًا وَاجْتَهَدَ فِي إِكْرَامِهِمَا فَأَقَامَا عِنْدَهُ بَقِيَّةَ لَيْلَتِهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahumā marḥaban wa-ahlan wa-ijtahada fī ikrāmihimā fa-aqāmā ʿindahu baqiyyata laylatihimā
sentences.l: So he said to-the-two: Welcome and family! And he-strove in honouring-the-two, and the-two-stayed with-him the rest of their-night.
sentences.i: He said to them, “Welcome, and be at home!” and did his utmost to honour them; and they stayed with him for the rest of the night.
sentences.n: marḥaban wa-ahlan, the greeting of welcome, is in the accusative of an unspoken verb: “(you have come to) a wide place and to family”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ خَرَجَا مِنْ عِنْدِهِ وَلَمْ يَزَالَا سَائِرَيْنِ حَتَّى وَصَلَا إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ وَدَخَلَاهَا وَجَازَا عَلَى بَيْتِ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ فَحَلَفَ عَلَى صَاحِبِهِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَأَدْخَلَهُ بَيْتَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu kharajā min ʿindihi wa-lam yazālā sāʾirayni ḥattā waṣalā ilā al-madīnati wa-dakhalāhā wa-jāzā ʿalā bayti Abī al-Ḥasani fa-ḥalafa ʿalā ṣāḥibihi ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-adkhalahu baytahu
sentences.l: And when the morning dawned, the-two went-out from beside-him, and the-two did-not cease going until they-two-reached to the city and entered-it, and passed by the house of Abū al-Ḥasan; and he-swore upon his-companion ʿAlī son of Bakkār and made-him-enter his-house.
sentences.i: When morning came they left him and walked on until they reached the city. They went in and passed by Abū al-Ḥasan's house, and he pressed his friend ʿAlī ibn Bakkār with an oath to come in, and took him inside.
sentences.n: min ʿindihi, “from his place”: ʿinda, “beside”, after min. lam yazālā sāʾirayni, “they did not cease going”: zāla with a negative means “to keep on”, and its predicate is accusative, here the dual sāʾirayni. jāza ʿalā, “to pass by”, is a later usage; the older is jāza bi- or marra bi-. ḥalafa ʿalā, “to swear upon someone”, is to press him with an oath so that he cannot refuse. adkhalahu baytahu, “made him enter his house”: form IV takes two objects.

sentences.t: فَاضْطَجَعَا عَلَى الْفِرَاشِ قَلِيلًا فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَا أَمَرَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ غِلْمَانَهُ أَنْ يَفْرِشُوا الْبَيْتَ بِالْفِرَاشَاتِ الْفَاخِرَةِ فَفَعَلُوا
sentences.tr: fa-iḍṭajaʿā ʿalā al-firāshi qalīlan fa-lammā afāqā amara Abū al-Ḥasani ghilmānahu an yafrishū al-bayta bi-al-firāshāti al-fākhirati fa-faʿalū
sentences.l: And the-two lay-down on the bedding a-little, and when they-two-came-to, Abū al-Ḥasan ordered his-servants that they-spread the room with the furnishings the splendid, and they-did.
sentences.i: The two of them lay down on the bedding for a while, and when they had come to themselves Abū al-Ḥasan ordered his servants to spread the room with splendid furnishings, and they did so.
sentences.n: The print runs Abū al-Ḥasan together here (ابوالحسن); it is kept and pointed as one word. amara … an yafrishū, “ordered … that they spread”: subjunctive after an, losing the -na of the plural. al-bayt here is the room they are in rather than the whole house. firāshāt, “bedding, furnishings”, is a later plural of firāsh (Classical furush); farasha … bi-, “to spread a place with”: bi- marks what is laid down.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ قَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَابُدَّأَنْ أُسَلِّيَ هَذَا الْغُلَامَ وَأُؤَانِسَهُ عَمَّا هُوَ فِيهِ فَإِنِّي أَدْرَيٰ بِحَالِهِ مِنْ غَيْرِي
sentences.tr: thumma inna Abā al-Ḥasani qāla fī nafsihi lā budda an usalliya hādhā al-ghulāma wa-uʾānisahu ʿammā huwa fīhi fa-innī adrā bi-ḥālihi min ghayrī
sentences.l: Then indeed Abū al-Ḥasan said in his-soul: (There is) no escape (but) that I-console this youth and keep-him-company from what he (is) in-it, for indeed I (am) more-knowing of his-state than other-than-me.
sentences.i: Then Abū al-Ḥasan said to himself, “I must cheer this young man and keep him company, to take his mind off his trouble, for I know how things stand with him better than anyone.”
sentences.n: After inna, “indeed”, the name takes the accusative: Abā al-Ḥasani, not Abū. The print runs lā budda, “no escape”, into an, “that” (لابدان); kept and pointed as one word. lā budda an, “it is unavoidable that”, i.e. “I must”, takes the subjunctive: usalliya … wa-uʾānisahu. sallā … ʿan, “to console someone from”: ʿammā is ʿan mā, “from what”. uʾānisu is form III of anisa, “to keep company, cheer”; the print sets its second hamza on wāw (اؤانسه). adrā bi-, “better acquainted with”, is the elative of darā, with bi- marking what is known and min, “than”, the comparison; the print writes its final alif as ي (ادري), shown here with a dagger alif. It could also be read adrī, “I know”, but min ghayrī, “than others”, calls for the comparative.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ اسْتَدْعَى بِمَاءٍ لِعَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ فَحَضَرُوا لَهُ بِالْمَاءِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Abā al-Ḥasani istadʿā bi-māʾin li-ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin fa-ḥaḍarū lahu bi-al-māʾi
sentences.l: Then indeed Abū al-Ḥasan called for water for ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and they-came to-him with the water.
sentences.i: Then Abū al-Ḥasan called for water for ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and the servants brought it to him.
sentences.n: istadʿā bi-, “to call for”: bi- marks what is sent for. li-ʿAliyyi, “for ʿAlī”: li- of the one it is meant for. ḥaḍarū lahu bi-al-māʾi, “they came to him with the water”: ḥaḍara bi-, “to come with”, does duty for “to bring”, where Classical usage prefers form IV aḥḍara; the subject, the servants, is left unstated.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ وَتَوَضَّأَ وَصَلَّى مَا فَاتَهُ مِنَ الْفُرُوضِ فِي يَوْمِهِ وَلَيْلَتِهِ وَجَلَسَ يُسَلِّى نَفْسَهُ مَعَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ بِالْكَلَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma wa-tawaḍḍaʾa wa-ṣallā mā fātahu mina al-furūḍi fī yawmihi wa-laylatihi wa-jalasa yusallī nafsahu maʿa Abū al-Ḥasani bi-al-kalāmi
sentences.l: And he-rose and performed-the-ablution and prayed what had-passed-him-by of the obligatory-prayers in his-day and his-night, and sat consoling himself with Abū al-Ḥasan with the talk.
sentences.i: Then he rose, made his ablutions and prayed the obligatory prayers he had missed that day and night, and sat with Abū al-Ḥasan, trying to take his mind off his grief in conversation.
sentences.n: mā fātahu, “what had passed him by”: the set prayers he had let go by while lying senseless, which he now makes up. yusallī nafsahu, “he consoled himself, diverted himself”, form II of salā, “to forget (a sorrow)”; the print writes it يسلّى with final ى for ي, its usual habit, and the shaddas of وصلّى and يسلّى are the print's own. maʿa Abū al-Ḥasan: after the preposition maʿa Classical Arabic wants the genitive Abī; the text keeps the nominative Abū, the name treated as a fixed form whatever its place in the sentence, a Middle Arabic habit, and it is pointed as it stands. The print runs the name together here (ابوالحسن). bi-al-kalāmi, “with talk”: bi- of the means.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى مِنْهُ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ ذَلِكَ تَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا سَيِّدِي إِنَّ الْأَلْيَقَ بِمَا أَنْتَ فِيهِ أَنْ تُقِيمَ عِنْدِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ لِيَنْشَرِحَ صَدْرُكَ وَيَنْفَرِجَ مَابِكَ مِنْ كَرْبِ الشَّوْقِ وَتَتَلَاهَى مَعَنَا لَعَلَّ أَنْ يَسْكُنَ مَا بِقَلْبِكَ مِنَ الْحُرَقِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā minhu Abū al-Ḥasani dhālika taqaddama ilayhi wa-qāla lahu yā sayyidī inna al-alyaqa bi-mā anta fīhi an tuqīma ʿindī hādhihi al-laylata li-yansharaḥa ṣadruka wa-yanfarija mā bika min karbi al-shawqi wa-tatalāhā maʿanā laʿalla an yaskuna mā bi-qalbika mina al-ḥuraqi
sentences.l: And when Abū al-Ḥasan saw that from-him, he-stepped-forward to-him and said to-him: O my-master, indeed the most-fitting for what you (are) in-it (is) that you-stay with-me this night, so-that your-breast may-open and what (is) with-you of the anguish of longing may-be-eased, and you-divert-yourself with-us; perhaps that what (is) in your-heart of the burnings may-grow-still.
sentences.i: When Abū al-Ḥasan saw this in him, he went up to him and said, “My master, the best thing for you in your present state is to stay with me tonight, so that your heart may be lightened and the anguish of longing that weighs on you be eased, and you may find some diversion in our company; perhaps the burning in your heart will grow still.”
sentences.n: The print has منة, a misprint for منه, corrected here. raʾā minhu dhālika, “saw that from him”: min marks the person in whom the thing shows. al-alyaq bi-, “most fitting for”: the elative of lāqa bi-, “to suit”, keeps its bi-; bi-mā anta fīhi, “for the state you are in”. li-yansharaḥa, “so that (your breast) may expand”: li- of purpose with the subjunctive, which carries on through yanfarija and tatalāhā; the opening of the breast is relief and good cheer. The print runs mā bika, “what is with you”, together (مابك). tatalāhā, form VI of lahā, “to amuse oneself, divert oneself”. laʿalla an yaskuna: laʿalla, “perhaps”, normally takes a noun or pronoun; here an and the subjunctive follow it, as after ʿasā, a construction of later prose. The shadda of لعلّ is the print's own. mā bi-qalbika, “what is in your heart”: bi- of place. ḥuraq, “burnings”, plural of ḥurqa, the fire of love.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ افْعَلْ يَا أَخِي مَا بَدَالَكَ فَإِنِّي عَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ غَيْرُ نَاجٍ مِمَّا أَصَابَنِي فَاصْنَعْ مَا أَنْتَ صَانِعٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin ifʿal yā akhī mā badā laka fa-innī ʿalā kulli ḥālin ghayru nājin mimmā aṣābanī fa-iṣnaʿ mā anta ṣāniʿun
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār said: Do, O my-brother, what has-appeared-good to-you; for I, upon every condition, (am) not escaping from-what has-befallen-me; so do what you (are) doing.
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said, “Do whatever you think best, my brother. Whatever happens, there is no escape for me from what has befallen me, so do as you will.”
sentences.n: mā badā laka, “whatever seems good to you”, printed run together (بدالك); li- marks the one to whom it seems. ʿalā kulli ḥālin, “in any case, whatever happens”. ghayru nājin, “not escaping”: nājin is the active participle of najā with its final -ī dropped in the indefinite, as with jārin in the last night. mimmā is min mā, “from what”. mā anta ṣāniʿun, “what you are doing”, that is, whatever you mean to do.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ وَاسْتَدْعَى غِلْمَانَهُ وَأَحْضَرَ بَعْضَ خَوَاصِّ أَصْحَابِهِ وَأَرْسَلَ إِلَى أَرْبَابِ الْمَغَانِي وَالْآلَاتِ فَحَضَرُوا
sentences.tr: fa-qāma Abū al-Ḥasani wa-istadʿā ghilmānahu wa-aḥḍara baʿḍa khawāṣṣi aṣḥābihi wa-arsala ilā arbābi al-maghānī wa-al-ālāti fa-ḥaḍarū
sentences.l: So Abū al-Ḥasan rose and summoned his-servants and brought some of the special-ones of his-companions, and sent to the masters of the songs and the instruments, and they-came.
sentences.i: So Abū al-Ḥasan rose, called his servants and fetched a few of his closest friends, and he sent for singers and musicians, and they came.
sentences.n: khawāṣṣ, “the special ones”, a man's intimates. arbāb al-maghānī wa-al-ālāt, “the masters of songs and of instruments”: arbāb, “lords, owners”, is used of those who practise a craft; maghānī is plural of maghnan, “singing”; ālāt, “instruments”, here musical ones. The madda of الآلات is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَهَيَّأَ لَهُمْ طَعَامًا وَشَرَابًا وَجَلَسُوا عَلَى أَكْلٍ وَشُرْبٍ وَانْشِرَاحٍ بَاقِيَ يَوْمِهِمْ إِلَى الْمَسَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-hayyaʾa lahum ṭaʿāman wa-sharāban wa-jalasū ʿalā aklin wa-shurbin wa-inshirāḥin bāqiya yawmihim ilā al-masāʾi
sentences.l: And he-made-ready for-them food and drink, and they-sat at eating and drinking and expansion (of heart) the remainder of their-day until the evening.
sentences.i: He had food and drink made ready for them, and they sat eating, drinking and making merry for the rest of the day until evening.
sentences.n: The shadda and hamza of هيّأ are the print's own. jalasū ʿalā, “they sat over” food and drink. inshirāḥ, “expansion”, the opening of the breast met just above, here merriment. bāqiya yawmihim, “the rest of their day”, accusative of time.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَوْقَدُوا الشُّمُوعَ وَدَارَتْ بَيْنَهُمْ كُؤُوسُ الْمُصَاحَبَةِ وَالْمُنَادَمَةِ فَطَابَ لَهُمُ الْوَقْتُ
sentences.tr: thumma awqadū al-shumūʿa wa-dārat baynahum kuʾūsu al-muṣāḥabati wa-al-munādamati fa-ṭāba lahumu al-waqtu
sentences.l: Then they-lit the candles, and there-went-round among-them the cups of companionship and drinking-fellowship, and the time became-sweet for-them.
sentences.i: Then they lit the candles, and the cups of good fellowship went round among them, and the hours passed sweetly.
sentences.n: al-muṣāḥaba wa-al-munādama, “companionship and drinking-fellowship”, a rhyming pair; munādama is keeping company over wine, from nadīm, a boon companion. ṭāba lahum al-waqt, “the time was good to them”: li- marks those who enjoy it; lahumu takes a helping -u before al-.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتِ الْمُغَنِّيَةُ الْعُودَ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhati al-mughanniyatu al-ʿūda wa-anshadat taqūlu
sentences.l: And the singing-girl took the lute and recited, saying:
sentences.i: The singing-girl took up the lute and sang:
sentences.n: The shadda of المغنّية is the print's own.

sentences.t:
رُمِيْتُ مِنَ الزَّمَانِ بِسَهْمِ لَحْظْ * فَاَصْمَانِي وَفَارَقْتُ الْحَبَائِبْ
وَعَانَدَنِي الزَّمَانُ وَقَلَّ صَبْرِي * وَاِنِّي قَبْلَ هٰذَا كُنْتُ حَبِيبْ
sentences.tr:
rumītu mina al-zamāni bi-sahmi laḥẓ * fa-aṣmānī wa-fāraqtu al-ḥabāʾib
wa-ʿānadanī al-zamānu wa-qalla ṣabrī * wa-innī qabla hādhā kuntu ḥabīb
sentences.l:
I-was-shot by Time with an arrow of a glance, * and it-struck-me-dead, and I-parted-from the loved-ones;
and Time set-itself-against-me, and my-patience grew-little, * and I, before this, was a beloved.
sentences.i:
Time shot me with the arrow of a glance, and the wound was mortal, and I was parted from those I love;
Time has turned against me and my patience has worn thin, though once, before all this, I was loved.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of فَاَصْمَانِي and وَاِنِّي, where the edition marks no hamza, and the pausal sukūn on the last word of the first hemistich and of each line (لَحْظْ, الْحَبَائِبْ, حَبِيبْ); the print also marks the long ī of رُمِيْتُ with sukūn. The metre is wāfir. rumītu, “I was shot”, is passive, with min marking who shoots, Time; bi-sahmi laḥẓ, “with the arrow of a glance”: bi- of the instrument, and the glance is the beloved's eye, love's stock arrow. aṣmā is said of a hunter whose shot kills the game where it stands; its subject is the arrow. ʿānada, “to oppose stubbornly”. The last word of line 2 stands where the type is damaged, and the reading ḥabīb is kept, though it sits awkwardly: “before this I was a beloved”, that is, once I too was loved, where one might expect the poet to say he was a lover. It keeps the rhyme letter b, but the long ī before it is not matched by line 1's -āʾib, and the closing foot does not scan as wāfir wants, so the word may well be corrupt; in prose the predicate of kuntu would be ḥabīban, and the pausal form hides the case.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ كَلَامَ الْمُغَنِّيَةِ وَقَعَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin kalāma al-mughanniyati waqaʿa ʿalā al-arḍi maghshiyyan ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And when ʿAlī son of Bakkār heard the words of the singing-girl, he-fell on the ground, swooned-upon.
sentences.i: When ʿAlī ibn Bakkār heard the singer's words, he fell to the ground in a swoon.
sentences.n: maghshiyyan ʿalayhi, “fainted”, literally “covered over”: the passive participle of ghashiya, a swoon having come over him, with ʿalayhi naming the one it covers; accusative of state. The shaddas of فلمّا, المغنّية and مغشيّا are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَزَلْ فِي غَشْيَتِهِ حَتَّى طَلَعَ الْفَجْرُ وَيَئِسَ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yazal fī ghashyatihi ḥattā ṭalaʿa al-fajru wa-yaʾisa Abū al-Ḥasani minhu
sentences.l: And he did-not cease in his-swoon until the dawn rose, and Abū al-Ḥasan despaired of-him.
sentences.i: He lay in his swoon until dawn broke, and Abū al-Ḥasan gave up hope for him.
sentences.n: lam yazal fī, “he did not cease (being) in”: he remained. yaʾisa min, “to despair of”; the hamza of يئس is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا لَمَعَ النَّهَارُ أَفَاقَ وَطَلَبَ الذَّهَابَ إِلَى بَيْتِهِ فَلَمْ يَمْنَعْهُ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ خَوْفًا مِنْ عَاقِبَةِ أَمْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā lamaʿa al-nahāru afāqa wa-ṭalaba al-dhahāba ilā baytihi fa-lam yamnaʿhu Abū al-Ḥasani khawfan min ʿāqibati amrihi
sentences.l: And when the day shone, he-came-to and sought the going to his-house; and Abū al-Ḥasan did-not hold-him-back, fearing from the outcome of his-affair.
sentences.i: When full daylight came he recovered his senses and asked to go home, and Abū al-Ḥasan did not keep him, fearing how the matter might end.
sentences.n: The print has خرنا, a misprint for خوفا, corrected here. afāqa, “to come to oneself” after a swoon or drunkenness. khawfan, “out of fear”, accusative of cause. ʿāqibat amrihi, “the outcome of his affair”: Abū al-Ḥasan fears what may come of keeping a man in this state in his house, and of an affair with one of the caliph's women.

sentences.t: فَأَتَاهُ غِلْمَانُهُ بِبَغْلَةٍ وَأَرْكَبُوهُ فَرَكِبَ وَسَارَ مَعَهُ أَبُوالْحَسَنِ وَبَعْضُ الْغِلْمَانِ إِلَى أَنْ أَدْخَلَهُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ مَنْزِلَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-atāhu ghilmānuhu bi-baghlatin wa-arkabūhu fa-rakiba wa-sāra maʿahu Abū al-Ḥasani wa-baʿḍu al-ghilmāni ilā an adkhalahu Abū al-Ḥasani manzilahu
sentences.l: And his-servants came-to-him with a she-mule and mounted-him, and he-rode; and there-went with-him Abū al-Ḥasan and some of the servants, until Abū al-Ḥasan brought-him-into his-dwelling.
sentences.i: His servants brought him a mule and set him on it, and he rode off, with Abū al-Ḥasan and some of the servants going with him, until Abū al-Ḥasan had brought him into his house.
sentences.n: atāhu … bi-baghlatin, “came to him with a mule”, that is, brought him one: atā bi- is “to bring”, the verb choosing the preposition. ghilmānuhu, “his servants”: the text leaves open whether they are ʿAlī's own or Abū al-Ḥasan's. arkabūhu, form IV of rakiba, “they set him riding”. ilā an with the perfect, “until”. From here the print sets the name as two words, ابو الحسن, where above it ran them together.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اطْمَأَنَّ فِي بَيْتِهِ حَمِدَ اللَّهَ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ عَلّى خَلَاصِهِ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْوَرْطَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā iṭmaʾanna fī baytihi ḥamida Allāha Abū al-Ḥasani ʿalā khalāṣihi min hādhihi al-warṭati
sentences.l: And when he-was-at-rest in his-house, Abū al-Ḥasan praised God for his-deliverance from this quagmire.
sentences.i: Once ʿAlī was safely settled in his own house, Abū al-Ḥasan thanked God that he was out of this predicament.
sentences.n: iṭmaʾanna, “to be at rest, settle down”; its subject is ʿAlī, and its hamza and shadda are the print's own, as is the shadda of فلمّا. The print sets a stray shadda on the preposition (علّى); it is kept, but the word is ʿalā, “for”, giving the cause of the praise (ḥamida ʿalā, “to praise for”). khalāṣihi, “his deliverance”, is most naturally Abū al-Ḥasan's own escape from the danger of ʿAlī dying under his roof, though it could be ʿAlī's safe return. warṭa, “a quagmire”, a plight one cannot easily get out of.

sentences.t: وَجَلَسَ مَعَهُ يُسَلِّيهِ وَهُوَ لَا يَمْلِكُ نَفْسَهُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْوَجْدِ وَالْغَرَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-jalasa maʿahu yusallīhi wa-huwa lā yamliku nafsahu min shiddati al-wajdi wa-al-gharāmi
sentences.l: And he-sat with-him consoling-him, while he does-not possess himself from the intensity of the passion and the love-longing.
sentences.i: He sat with him, trying to comfort him, but ʿAlī could not master himself for the violence of his passion and longing.
sentences.n: The print has ننسه, a misprint for نفسه, corrected here. wa-huwa, “while he”, opens a circumstantial clause, and huwa is now ʿAlī. lā yamliku nafsahu, “he does not own himself”, cannot control himself. min shiddati, “from the intensity”: min of cause. wajd and gharām are both words for consuming love. The shadda of يسلّيه is the print's own, and here the print writes the final ي, against يسلّى above.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ وَوَدَّعَهُ وَانْصَرَفَ إِلَى مَنْزِلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma Abū al-Ḥasani wa-waddaʿahu wa-inṣarafa ilā manzilihi
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan rose and bade-him-farewell and departed to his-dwelling.
sentences.i: Then Abū al-Ḥasan rose, took his leave of him, and went home.
sentences.n: The shadda of ودّعه is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
